name: Ndebele dzilla neck rings

lead: Dzilla (also spelled idzila) are stacked metal neck rings traditionally worn by married women among the South Ndebele. Husbands gave them to wives, and they signalled marital commitment and the household's means.

The visual effect is a longer, column-like neck. Descriptions of similar neck-ring traditions say the stretch is largely an illusion created by rings pressing the collarbone and ribs downward rather than lengthened vertebrae.

paras: Rings, usually copper or brass and often stacked in multiples of three, were added over the years of marriage and worn together with arm and leg rings, beadwork and head coverings. Permanent wearing is no longer common today.

Wikipedia notes the rings are not described as a neck-stretching modification. Heavy permanent rings are described by popular sources as weighty; health outcomes are not well documented in the sources consulted.

angle.text: The rings change how the neck looks while worn, creating a stacked, elongated line. Their purpose is cultural display of marriage and status.

lead: Dzilla (idzila) are copper or brass rings worn by married women of the South Ndebele people of South Africa, as part of traditional dress. [1] They are given by husbands and kept, according to Wikipedia, until the husband dies. [1] They are associated with wealth, status and fidelity. [2]

As an appearance practice the rings create an elongated, stacked neck line, part of a wider ornamentation of married women that includes beaded headbands and headdresses, a beaded apron and a beadwork blanket. [2] Wikipedia notes that the rings 'do not function as a body modification' and that, in discussions of neck rings in other cultures, the elongation effect is described as largely illusory because the rings' weight pushes the collarbone and upper ribs down. [1]
Sources agree the practice has declined and that permanent wearing is no longer common; some describe lighter replacements made of other materials. [2]
infobox: Copper or brass, often stacked in threes [1]

paras: Dzilla are rings of copper or brass, typically stacked in multiples of three, and worn around the neck, arms and legs. [1] Wearing them signalled a woman's married status; the number reflected the husband's means. [2]

Kruger Park's cultural summary describes the rings as symbolising a wife's bond and faithfulness to her husband, to be removed only upon his death. [2] Ndebele women also wore beaded head coverings, a five-fingered apron (ijogolo) marking completion of marriage after the first child, and a beaded marriage blanket (nguba). [2] Women's ornaments signalled social status and dress grew more elaborate after marriage. [2]

Wikipedia describes neck-ring elongation, in connection with Kayan women, as mostly illusory because the weight shifts the collarbone and ribs downward, not because vertebrae lengthen. [1] It states that Ndebele rings do not function as a body modification. [1]
Permanent wearing is no longer common, according to Kruger Park's summary. [2] Beadwork and related crafts continue, and many pieces are now made for sale. [2]
